vignette: Meet Leela, a 20-year-old South Eastern Asian soldier who has been married for two years. Her life took a drastic turn when she was assaulted by a fellow soldier during a training exercise. The event left her with a deep sense of shame and disconnection from her community and culture. Leela often finds herself overeating to distract herself from the memories of that fateful day. She eats more than usual, hoping to feel better, but it only provides temporary relief. "I just can't believe someone else wouldn't have stopped it," she says, her voice laced with self-doubt. This notion that others would have coped better has become a recurring theme in her thoughts, leading her to question her own strength and resilience. As a result, she redirects her attention to other things, trying to avoid the painful memories altogether. However, these memories persist, haunting her in vivid images and pictures. The memory feels alien, as if it belongs to someone else, and Leela struggles to reconcile it with her sense of self. "It's like watching a movie," she says, "I see myself in it, but I don't feel connected to the person on screen." This disconnection from her memories has led her to overanalyse every detail of the event, hoping to make sense of what happened. She replays the images in her mind, trying to identify what she could have done differently. Leela's negative appraisals about herself and others have become a self-reinforcing cycle. Her conviction that someone else would have stopped the assault has led her to feel like a failure, which in turn fuels her maladaptive strategies of overeating and redirection. "I'm not the person I used to be," she laments. "I've lost touch with my community and culture; I don't know who I am anymore." Her sense of unrecognisable self has become a constant source of distress. As Leela tries to navigate her emotions, she finds herself trapped in a cycle of avoidance and negative thinking. Her maladaptive strategies have become a way to cope with the memories, but they also perpetuate them, making it harder for her to move on. "I feel like I'm stuck in this never-ending loop," she says, frustration etched on her face. Leela's daily life as a soldier has been significantly impacted by these symptoms. She struggles to connect with her fellow soldiers, feeling like an outsider among people who were once her friends and comrades. Her marriage is also suffering, as her husband tries to be supportive but doesn't know how to reach out to the person she used to be. Leela's current state is one of desperation. She feels overwhelmed by her memories and negative appraisals, and her maladaptive strategies are no longer providing relief. "I just want to feel like myself again," she says, tears streaming down her face. "I want to reconnect with my community and culture; I want to be able to look at myself in the mirror without feeling ashamed."
